title: I am the resurrection (John 11:17–27)
hookLine: grieving Martha makes a great confession of faith
tomorrow: The house filled with the odor

lines: MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.
cards: At hospital bedsides and after funerals, one sentence keeps coming back. If only. If only the ambulance had come sooner.
If only I'd called. If only you'd been here. It isn't really a question, and it isn't quite blame.
It's love with nowhere to go. In Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, a man named Lazarus has died, and his sister Martha hears that Jesus is finally on the road. She doesn't wait at the house.
She goes out to meet him, and the first thing she says is that sentence.

teach.b: Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days. Friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. Mary stays sitting in the house; Martha gets up and goes.

She says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." In the same breath she adds that even now she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Grief and trust, side by side.
Jesus tells her, your brother will rise again. She answers like a believer of her time: I know he will rise again at the resurrection on the last day. True, but far off.
Then Jesus pulls the far-off thing into the present tense: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live."
Not, I will bring the resurrection someday. I am it, standing here. He asks her straight out: believest thou this?
And Martha, still grieving, answers with a full confession of faith: yea, Lord, I have believed that thou art Christ the Son of the living God.
Some readers set it beside Peter's confession in Matthew, which uses the same titles.
Here it comes from a grieving woman on the road outside her village. Luke remembers Martha as the busy sister who asked Jesus to send Mary to help her serve.

John shows her another way: the one who walks out to meet him and says who he is. The Church offers these words among the readings for funeral Masses, and keeps one memorial for Martha, Mary and Lazarus together.

how: John 11 is among the Gospel readings the Church provides for funeral Masses, and Catholics pray for their dead by name, especially in November and on the anniversary of a death.

o: the weeping of mourners at a burial
a long rest in the tomb before the end

s: Martha only appears in the Gospels as the busy one in the kitchen
in John 11 she says: thou art Christ the Son of the living God.
Martha already believed in a resurrection on the last day
she says so; Jesus answers, I am the resurrection.
Martha's first words to Jesus mix grief and trust
if thou hadst been here, then: even now God will give thee what thou ask.

games.q: you're Martha. your brother has been dead four days, and Jesus has finally arrived. what do you do?
o: stay in the house with the mourners.
go out to meet him on the road.
send word that it's too late.
games.why: Martha goes out to meet him while Mary stays in the house. on that road she says, thou art Christ the Son of the living God.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, someone you hardly knew but think about, and see their face, their handwriting, the chair they sat in; if there's an if only, let it be there without fixing it.
If you pray, say Martha's words for them, or Jesus's: I am the resurrection and the life. If you don't pray, simply hold their name and let it rest in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Anastasis. The Greek word for resurrection, literally a standing up again: what Jesus told Martha he was, standing right in front of her. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the resurrection, literally a standing up again (John 11:25).

carryVoice: Your line: love with nowhere to go. Martha carried hers out to the road, and met him there. Go gently.
